newsitem.title: HUNGARY: EMU INFLATION AIMS SEEN TOO TIGHT FOR NEW EU MEMBERS.
newsitem.headline: EMU INFLATION AIMS SEEN TOO TIGHT FOR NEW EU MEMBERS.

text.p: The head of Hungary's central bank told an international conference on global convergence that the European Union cannot expect new members from Central Europe to meet Maastricht criteria on inflation "in the foreseeable future".
"I want to emphasise Hungary's commitment to meeting the convergence criteria for Maastricht," Gyorgy Suranyi said on Thursday.

"At the same time...certain criteria cannot be met in the short-term -- if inflation is going to be fluctuating between one and two percent in the European Union this is something that is unrealistic in the foreseeable future from the point of view of the transition countries."

Suranyi was addressing a conference organised by the Robert Triffin-Szirak Foundation and the European research organistion SUERF to mark the 50th annoversary of the Marshall Plan, the United States' massive post World War Two aid package for Europe.

Suranyi told Reuters that in post-communist economies productivity in the tradeable sector was increasing quickly, producing a higher rate of growth than in matured market economies and an accompanying rise in nominal wages.

"This is a pre-requisite of catching up," he said. "However, this means that nominal wage growth, bearing in mind that there is a downward rigidity in nominal wages, is going to correspond with the productivity growth."
"So all in all due to the close linkage between productivity growth and nominal wage hikes and the unified labour market, inflation has to be inevitably somewhat higher (than in matured economies)."

Suranyi said that while year-on-year inflation in Hungary, currently at 18.6 percent, was too high, he was satisfied both with the direction of inflation, which had come down from a peak of 31 percent at the end of 1995, and with evidence that the downward trend was sustainable.

"For the first time for two or three decades there is no trade-off between the deceleration of inflation and the deterioration of the external balances," he said. "Just the contrary, while inflation is decelerating both the fiscal and external stability has strengthened quite substantially."

The country's fiscal deficit has been cut from nine percent of GDP to around four percent while the current account deficit has been reduced from 9.4 percent to around 3.6 percent at the end of 1996, Suranyi told the delegates of European bankers and economists.
Suranyi said Hungary's high inflation had been an unavoidable consequence of a series of major economic structural adjustments after the end of communism.
He compared Hungary's position with that of the developed economies in the 1970s after the disruption caused by sharp rises in oil prices in 1973.

"If I refer to the major market economies in the 1970s, one single energy price shock accelerated the rate of infation quite substantially with many of those countries experiencing double digit inflation," Suranyi said.

"It we look at our shocks -- our (former Soviet and East European) export market collapsed, the ownership structure was absolutely reshuffled, domestic demand dropped dramatically and the whole external and internal trade has been restructured -- it is really not a surprise that inflation has accelerated, it was impossible to avoid."
